mainTopic: The meaning of שכר and תירוש, the two faces of wine, and the sources that refraining from anointing and bathing counts as עינוי on יום הכפורים.
overview: This amud finishes a proof about the word שכר. It rejects the idea that sweet dried figs are included and learns from נזיר through a גזירה שוה that שכר means wine. The גמרא then asks whether תירוש means wine. A ברייתא about vows suggests it does not. The גמרא deflects two פסוקים, but a third, ״זנות ויין ותירוש יקח לב״, settles it: everyone agrees תירוש is wine in the פסוקים, and for vows we follow everyday speech. Wordplays on יין and תירוש, together with teachings of רב כהנא and רבא, show that wine can harm a person or raise him up, depending on whether he is worthy. Next the גמרא asks how we know that holding back from סיכה and רחיצה counts as עינוי on יום הכפורים. It proves anointing from דניאל's fast and the angel's word 'ולהתענות'. רב זוטרא's proof for bathing from תהלים is challenged by a משנה, so רב אשי learns bathing from ״וסוך לא סכתי״ itself. Finally, the גמרא asks what the angel meant by 'I have come because of your words' and begins an answer from יחזקאל's vision, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the source: he is liable
steps.stepSummary: The last word of a source quoted on the previous amud. It says that someone who ate sweet dried figs and entered the מקדש is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: (He is liable.)
steps.whatsHappening: This single word finishes an earlier proof. That proof suggested a כהן is liable for eating sweet dried figs before entering the מקדש, so שכר might include figs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a כהן is liable for figs under the rule of 'יין ושכר אל תשת', then שכר seems to mean anything that intoxicates, even food. This possibility is set up only so the גמרא can reject it in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Sweet dried figs from קעילה, thought to make a person drunk

phrases.english: (is liable).
phrases.notes: This word finishes a teaching that started on the previous amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a proof earlier.
steps.raayaObject: That שכר can include intoxicating food such as sweet dried figs.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A source ruling that one who ate דבילה קעילית and entered the מקדש is liable.

steps.title: Rather, שכר means wine, learned from נזיר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the fig idea. It learns through a גזירה שוה from נזיר that שכר means wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, we learn the word 'שכר' here from the word 'שכר' said about a נזיר. Just as there it means wine, so too here it means wine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says 'אלא' ('rather') to throw out the previous idea. It explains that שכר means wine, not figs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same word, שכר, appears in the laws of the כהן and in the laws of נזיר. Through a גזירה שוה, the clear meaning in נזיר (wine) is carried over to the כהן. So the כהן's prohibition is about strong wine, not sweet figs.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; this throws out the previous idea
A person who vowed to stay away from wine and grape products
Just as there, so too here; the formula of a גזירה שוה

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how a גזירה שוה can fix the meaning of an unclear word by using a place where its meaning is clear.

phrases.english: Rather:
we derive 'sheikhar' 'sheikhar' from the nazirite,
phrases.notes: This is a גזירה שוה: the same word appears in both places, so we learn one from the other.

phrases.english: just as there it is wine,
so too here it is wine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the fig reading built in step 1.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea that שכר includes sweet dried figs.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A גזירה שוה from נזיר shows that שכר means wine specifically.
steps.whatToRemember: שכר in the כהן's prohibition means wine, learned from נזיר through a גזירה שוה.

steps.title: Is תירוש really wine? A vow suggests not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions whether תירוש means wine. It cites a ברייתא: one who vows off תירוש is forbidden in sweet foods but allowed to drink wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is תירוש wine? But a ברייתא teaches: one who vows not to have תירוש is forbidden in all kinds of sweet foods but is allowed wine!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the word תירוש and challenges the idea that it means wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vows follow how people ordinarily use words. If someone who swore off תירוש may still drink wine, then people do not use 'תירוש' to mean wine. Instead it seems to mean sweet things.

keyTerms.meaning: Usually translated 'new wine'; its exact meaning is the question here
But a ברייתא teaches; this introduces a challenge

steps.confusionAlert: Vows are decided by how ordinary people talk. So this ברייתא is evidence about everyday meaning. It does not necessarily tell us how the תורה uses the word.

phrases.english: And is tirosh wine?
But isn't it taught:
one who vows off tirosh
is forbidden in all kinds of sweet foods
and is permitted wine!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to an earlier topic: the meaning of תירוש.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that תירוש means wine.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A vow off תירוש does not forbid wine, so תירוש must mean something other than wine.

steps.title: But a פסוק says תירוש makes maidens speak
steps.stepSummary: A counter-challenge: the פסוק 'ותירוש ינובב בתולות' implies that תירוש intoxicates, so it must be wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: And is it not wine? But it is written: 'And תירוש makes the maidens speak.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against the ברייתא with a פסוק that seems to show תירוש is wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ינובב is related to ניב, speech. Something that loosens the tongues of even modest maidens sounds like an intoxicating drink, and sweet foods do not do that. So the פסוק seems to treat תירוש as wine.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is written; this introduces a challenge from a פסוק
Makes speak, makes flourish (from ניב, speech)

phrases.english: And is it not wine?
But isn't it written:
'And tirosh shall make the maidens speak',

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion of step 3 that תירוש is not wine.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion from the ברייתא that תירוש is not wine.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only an intoxicating drink would make maidens speak, so תירוש in the פסוק must be wine.

steps.title: It means something that comes from תירוש
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: the פסוק means that what comes from תירוש, meaning wine, makes maidens speak.
steps.simpleTranslation: Something that comes from תירוש makes the maidens speak.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads the פסוק a different way so that it no longer proves תירוש is wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תירוש itself could be sweet grapes or juice. The wine made from it is what makes people speak. The פסוק names the source (תירוש) but means its product (wine), so the ברייתא still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Something that comes from; a product of

phrases.english: Something that comes from tirosh
makes the maidens speak.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from זכריה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק calls תירוש itself an intoxicant.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק refers to wine made from תירוש. תירוש itself is not wine.

steps.title: But a פסוק says the vats overflow with תירוש
steps.stepSummary: A second challenge: 'ותירוש יקביך יפרוצו' seems to show that תירוש is the wine filling the vats.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written: 'And your vats will overflow with תירוש'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another פסוק that seems to prove תירוש is wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vats (יקבים) hold pressed wine. If תירוש overflows the vats, it sounds like תירוש is the wine itself.

phrases.english: But isn't it written:
'And your vats shall overflow with tirosh'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new פסוק challenging the answer in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that תירוש is not wine.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Wine vats are filled with wine, so the תירוש that fills them must be wine.

steps.title: Again, what comes from תירוש fills the vats
steps.stepSummary: The same answer: what comes from תירוש, meaning wine, overflows the vats.
steps.simpleTranslation: Something that comes from תירוש makes your vats overflow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the same method as before to answer the second פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Plenty of תירוש (grapes) produces wine that overflows the vats. The פסוק describes the result of having lots of תירוש. It does not say that תירוש itself is wine.
steps.whatToRemember: So far, both פסוקים are deflected by reading them as 'something that comes from תירוש.' This is not the final word. The next step brings a פסוק that cannot be deflected this way, and step 9 concludes that תירוש does mean wine.

phrases.english: Something that comes from tirosh
makes your vats overflow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from משלי, using the same method as step 5.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The vats are filled with תירוש itself, so it is wine.
steps.terutzMaskana: The vats are filled with wine produced from תירוש.

steps.title: A third verse shows תירוש makes a person drunk
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings ״זנות ויין ותירוש יקח לב״ as a strong challenge against the idea that תירוש is not wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written: "Harlotry, and wine, and תירוש take away the heart"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more פסוק to show that תירוש really is wine. This one cannot easily be answered the way the last two were.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In steps 5 and 7, the גמרא escaped by saying 'what comes from תירוש.' Here, though, the פסוק says that תירוש itself 'takes away the heart,' meaning it confuses the mind. Only an intoxicating drink does that, so תירוש must be wine.

keyTerms.meaning: Takes away the heart, clouds a person's judgment
But it is written (introduces a challenge from a פסוק)

phrases.english: But it is written
"Harlotry, and wine, and tirosh take away the heart"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third proof that תירוש is wine, after the earlier answers covered the first two פסוקים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading, based on the ברייתא, that תירוש is not wine.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק says that תירוש itself clouds the mind. That describes an intoxicating drink, which means wine.

steps.title: תירוש is wine in the תורה, but נדרים follow everyday speech
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that everyone agrees תירוש means wine in the פסוקים. The ברייתא rules differently only because נדרים follow ordinary language.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, everyone agrees that תירוש is wine, and in vows we follow the way people speak.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up its pushback and accepts that תירוש means wine. It then explains why the ברייתא about vows still says otherwise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no real argument about what the word means in the תורה: it means wine. In the time of the ברייתא, however, people used the word תירוש for sweet foods and not for wine. A נדר is judged by what the person meant, so his everyday language decides the case.

keyTerms.term: בִּנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם
keyTerms.meaning: For vows, follow how people commonly speak

steps.whatToRemember: תירוש means wine in the תורה. A person who makes a נדר using the word תירוש is judged by everyday speech, so wine is still permitted to him.
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא does not prove that תירוש is not wine in the תורה. It only shows what the word meant in common speech when a person made a נדר.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic rule across all of נדרים: we follow what the speaker meant in his own language, not the meaning in the פסוקים.

phrases.english: Rather, according to everyone
tirosh is wine

phrases.aramaic: וּבִנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם.
phrases.english: and in vows, follow the language of people

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge of step 8 and resolves the ברייתא from step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting contexts: the meaning in the פסוקים versus the meaning in ordinary speech for נדרים.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to show that the word תירוש does not mean wine.
steps.terutzMaskana: תירוש is wine in the תורה. The ברייתא reflects only how people spoke when making נדרים.

steps.title: Why does wine have two names?
steps.stepSummary: Since יין and תירוש are the same thing, the גמרא asks why the תורה uses two different names.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why is it called יין, and why is it called תירוש?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question. If both words mean wine, what does each name teach? This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that תירוש is established as wine, having two names seems unnecessary. The גמרא assumes each name carries its own lesson.

phrases.english: And why does it call it yayin (wine)
and why does it call it tirosh?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the conclusion that both names refer to wine.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What lesson each of the two names for wine teaches.

steps.title: יין brings wailing; תירוש brings poverty
steps.stepSummary: יין sounds like יללה (wailing), and תירוש contains the word רש (poor). Both names warn against wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: יין, because it brings wailing to the world. תירוש, because anyone who indulges in it becomes poor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a wordplay on each name. Both are warnings about the dangers of wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יין is linked to יללה, the crying that comes from the sins and troubles caused by drunkenness. תירוש is read as containing רש, meaning poor, because heavy drinking leads to ruin.

keyTerms.meaning: One who indulges in it, gets too involved with it

phrases.english: Yayin — because it brings wailing to the world
Tirosh — because anyone who indulges in it
becomes poor

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each name is a wordplay warning: יין leads to יללה, and תירוש leads to being רש.

steps.title: רב כהנא: תירוש can make a person a head or a pauper
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא notes that the word is written תירש but read תירוש. If a person is worthy, wine makes him a ראש; if not, it makes him רש.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא pointed out a contrast: it is written 'תירש' and we read 'תירוש.' If one merits, he becomes a head; if not, he becomes poor.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא adds to the last step. He shows that wine is not only harmful: it can lift a person up or bring him down, depending on whether he is worthy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The written form, תירש, hints at רש (poor). The read form, תירוש, hints at ראש (head). Having both forms teaches that wine can lead to either result, depending on how worthy the person is and how he drinks.

keyTerms.meaning: It is written one way and read another way (כתיב and קרי)
If he merits, if he is worthy

phrases.english: Rav Kahana raised a contrast:
It is written 'tirash,' and we read 'tirosh'
If he merits — he becomes a head
If he does not merit — he becomes poor

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a softer view to step 11: wine can also bring greatness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wine raises a worthy person and brings down an unworthy one.

steps.title: רבא: wine can bring joy or confusion
steps.stepSummary: רבא makes a similar point about ״ישמח״, which is written with a שׁ and read with a שׂ. Wine makes a worthy person happy and leaves an unworthy one confused.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the same as רבא's teaching, for רבא pointed out a contrast: it is written 'יְשַׁמַּח' (with שׁ) and we read 'יְשַׂמַּח' (with שׂ). If one merits, it makes him happy; if not, it leaves him confused.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רבא taught the same idea as רב כהנא, using a different פסוק about wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק ״ויין ישמח לבב אנוש״ can be read with שׂ, meaning שמחה (joy), or with שׁ, meaning שממה (being confused or desolate). Like רב כהנא, רבא learns that the effect of wine depends on whether the person is worthy.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is the same as
Makes him confused, leaves him dazed

phrases.english: (And this is the same as Rava's teaching, for Rava) raised a contrast
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets, the ones that tie this to רב כהנא's teaching.

phrases.english: It is written 'yeshamach' (with shin), and we read 'yesamach' (with sin)
If he merits — it makes him happy
If he does not merit — it makes him confused

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel teaching that matches רב כהנא's idea.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wine brings joy to the worthy and confusion to the unworthy.

steps.title: רבא: wine and fragrances make me wise
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא connects this to another saying of רבא: wine and good scents sharpen my mind.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what רבא said: Wine and fragrances make me wise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another saying of רבא that fits the idea that wine helps someone who is worthy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא describes wine as helping his own clear thinking. This matches the 'זכה' side of the teaching: for a worthy person, wine is a benefit.

keyTerms.meaning: Make me wise, sharpen my mind

steps.whatToRemember: Wine has two sides. It can bring wailing and poverty, or it can bring greatness, joy, and wisdom, depending on the person.

phrases.english: And this is what Rava said:
Wine and fragrances — make me wise

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the 'זכה' side of רבא's teaching in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: That wine benefits a worthy person.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבא's own statement that wine and fragrances make him wise.

steps.title: How do we know bathing and anointing count as affliction?
steps.stepSummary: A new section begins. The גמרא asks for the source that holding back from רחיצה and סיכה is called עינוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Bathing and anointing: from where do we know that holding back from them is called affliction?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic among the יום כיפור restrictions. It asks for a source and sets up the proof that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה commands ״ועניתם את נפשותיכם״. The גמרא already discussed eating and drinking; now it wants to show that not washing and not anointing also count as עינוי.

phrases.english: Bathing and anointing
from where do we know that it is called affliction?

steps.triggerLanguage: רְחִיצָה וְסִיכָה, מְנָא לַן דְּאִיקְּרִי עִינּוּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. It leaves the discussion of wine and returns to the list of יום כיפור restrictions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source showing that refraining from רחיצה and סיכה counts as עינוי.

steps.title: The verse about דניאל's fast
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites דניאל, who describes holding back from pleasant bread, meat, wine, and anointing during his time of affliction.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: "I ate no pleasant bread, neither did meat nor wine enter my mouth, neither did I anoint myself at all."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק where דניאל lists the things he gave up while afflicting himself. Not anointing is one of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because דניאל lists not anointing together with his self-affliction, we see that holding back from סיכה is a form of עינוי. This פסוק mentions only anointing; the proof for bathing comes later.

keyTerms.meaning: And I did not anoint myself at all

phrases.english: As it is written:
"I ate no pleasant bread

phrases.aramaic: וּבָשָׂר וָיַיִן לֹא בָא אֶל פִּי
phrases.english: and meat and wine did not enter my mouth
and I did not anoint myself at all"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: דניאל's account of his affliction includes not anointing, so refraining from סיכה counts as עינוי.

steps.title: What is 'pleasant bread'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pauses to ask what ״לחם חמודות״ in the פסוק means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the meaning of "I ate no pleasant bread"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a side question to explain one phrase in the פסוק. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is unclear which bread counts as 'pleasant.' The גמרא wants to know exactly what דניאל gave up.

phrases.english: What is the meaning of "I ate no pleasant bread"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains a phrase in the פסוק cited in step 16.

steps.title: דניאל did not even eat refined wheat bread
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה בריה דרב שמואל בר שילת explains that דניאל did not even eat bread made of fine, clean wheat.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה, son of רב שמואל בר שילת, said: He did not even eat bread made from refined wheat.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא explains the phrase: 'pleasant bread' means bread made from fine, sifted wheat, and דניאל did not eat even that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דניאל gave up not only luxuries but even ordinary good-quality bread. He ate only coarse bread with the bran mixed in. This shows how strictly he afflicted himself.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר שִׁילַת:
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda, son of Rav Shmuel bar Sheilat, said:
Even bread of refined wheat
he did not eat

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר שִׁילַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״לחם חמודות״ means bread made of refined wheat, and דניאל did not eat even that.

steps.title: How do we know דניאל's holding back counts as affliction?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know that what דניאל did is called עינוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know that this is considered affliction?
steps.whatsHappening: The פסוק the גמרא quoted earlier (דניאל י:ג) only lists what דניאל held back from. It never uses the word 'affliction.' So the גמרא now asks how we know his holding back counts as עינוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof from דניאל only helps us for יום הכפורים if what he did is called עינוי, because that is the word the תורה uses. The earlier פסוק only lists what he held back from and does not name it. So the גמרא needs one more link to connect דניאל's holding back to the word עינוי.

keyTerms.meaning: Affliction (the תורה's word for the fast of יום הכפורים)

phrases.english: And from where do we know that it is considered affliction?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the main proof from דניאל (step 16), after the short side question about לחם חמודות (steps 17-18).
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Proof that דניאל's holding back from food, wine and anointing is called עינוי.

steps.title: The angel tells דניאל he afflicted himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the angel, who says that דניאל 'afflicted himself' during that same time.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'Then he said to me: Do not be afraid, דניאל, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and to afflict yourself before your God, your words were heard, and I have come because of your words.' ('For you are greatly loved.')
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק in which the angel tells דניאל that he 'afflicted himself' (וּלְהִתְעַנּוֹת). So the holding back described earlier is called עינוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This פסוק is in the same chapter as the earlier one and describes the same period. The angel calls that period 'afflicting yourself.' So the mourning-style holding back, including no anointing, is a kind of עינוי. The words in parentheses come from a different פסוק and seem to be an added note.

keyTerms.meaning: And to afflict yourself (same root as עינוי)

phrases.english: As it is written: 'And he said to me: Do not be afraid, Daniel,
for from the first day
that you set your heart to understand
and to afflict yourself before your God,
phrases.notes: The key word here is להתענות, which comes from the same root as עינוי.

phrases.english: your words were heard,
and I have come because of your words.'
phrases.notes: The גמרא will come back to explain this phrase in step 27.

phrases.english: ('For you are greatly loved.')
phrases.notes: This is from דניאל 9:23. Some versions leave out these words in round brackets.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The angel calls דניאל's behavior 'להתענות', so holding back from anointing counts as עינוי.

steps.title: Anointing is covered, but where is bathing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says we have found a source for סיכה, and now asks for a source for רחיצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have found a source for anointing. From where do we know bathing?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notes that דניאל's פסוק clearly mentions anointing, but not bathing. So it asks for a separate source that holding back from bathing is also עינוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק 'וסוך לא סכתי' only talks about anointing with oil. Bathing is a different activity. It is also forbidden on יום הכפורים, so it needs its own source.

phrases.english: We have found anointing;
bathing, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the proof for סיכה and asks the same question about רחיצה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that holding back from bathing is called עינוי.

steps.title: רב זוטרא: water is compared to oil
steps.stepSummary: רב זוטרא בריה דרבי טוביה quotes a פסוק that puts water and oil side by side, so bathing is like anointing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זוטרא, son of רבי טוביה, said: The פסוק says: 'And it came into his insides like water, and like oil into his bones.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב זוטרא answers with a פסוק from תהלים that mentions water and oil together. He reads the water as bathing water that soaks into the body, just like oil does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק links water and oil as two things that enter the body. Since holding back from oil is already called עינוי, holding back from water used for bathing is treated the same way.

phrases.english: Rav Zutra, son of Rabbi Toviya, said:
The verse says: 'And it came into his insides like water,'
'and like oil into his bones.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב זוּטְרָא בְּרַבִּי טוֹבִיָּה, אָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about bathing.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The water in תהלים 109:18 is put together with oil, so bathing is like anointing and holding back from it is עינוי.

steps.title: Maybe the water means drinking
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: perhaps 'water into his insides' means drinking, not bathing.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say that it means drinking!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: water that goes 'into his insides' sounds like drinking. If so, the פסוק says nothing about bathing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'insides' (בקרבו) naturally suggests swallowing. If the water is drunk, the פסוק no longer proves anything about bathing.

phrases.english: But say it refers to drinking!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב זוטרא's reading of the פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב זוטרא's reading of the water as bathing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Into his insides' suggests drinking, so the פסוק may not be about bathing at all.

steps.title: The water is like the oil: used on the outside
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the water is like the oil next to it, and oil is used on the outside of the body.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is similar to oil: just as oil is used from the outside, so too water is used from the outside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב זוטרא. The water should be read like the oil in the same פסוק. Oil is smeared on the outside of the body, so the water is also used on the outside, which means bathing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two halves of the פסוק go together. Since the oil is clearly for anointing, the water must also be something put on the body from outside. That makes it bathing, not drinking.

phrases.english: It is like oil:
just as oil is from the outside,
so too water is from the outside.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the two halves of the פסוק as matching each other
steps.terutzMaskana: The water matches the oil, which is used on the outside, so it means bathing.

steps.title: A משנה reads the פסוק the opposite way
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: a תנא uses the same פסוק to show that anointing is like drinking, so the water must mean drinking.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the תנא takes it the opposite way, as we learned: From where do we know that anointing is like drinking on יום הכפורים? Even though there is no proof for the matter, there is a hint to the matter, as it says: 'And it came into his insides like water, and like oil into his bones.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה that uses this same פסוק to show that anointing counts like drinking. That only works if the water in the פסוק is drunk water, which goes against רב זוטרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב זוטרא read the water to match the oil, meaning both are on the outside. The תנא reads it the other way: the oil is compared to the water, and the water is drunk. Since a תנא has more authority than an אמורא, רב זוטרא's reading is in trouble.

keyTerms.meaning: A hint for the matter (not a full proof)

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides use the exact same פסוק. The only question is which half explains the other. רב זוטרא says the water is like the oil, used on the outside. The משנה says the oil is like the water, which is drunk.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא תַּנָּא אִיפְּכָא קָא נָסֵיב לַהּ,
phrases.english: But the tanna takes it the opposite way,
as we learned: From where do we know that anointing
is like drinking on Yom Kippur?

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין רְאָיָה לַדָּבָר,
phrases.english: Even though there is no proof for the matter,
there is a hint to the matter,
as it says: 'And it came into his insides like water,'
'and like oil into his bones!'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא תַּנָּא אִיפְּכָא קָא נָסֵיב לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a stronger challenge against רב זוטרא's answer, even after step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב זוטרא's reading of the water as bathing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה reads the water as drinking and compares the oil to it, which is the reverse of רב זוטרא's reading.

steps.title: רב אשי: bathing comes from דניאל's own פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי drops the תהלים proof and says bathing is learned from 'וסוך לא סכתי' itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אשי said: Bathing is learned from the פסוק itself, as it is written: 'And I did not anoint myself at all.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up on רב זוטרא's proof. רב אשי says the same words in דניאל, 'וסוך לא סכתי', already include bathing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'אלא' (rather) shows that the earlier answer is set aside. רב אשי reads 'וסוך לא סכתי' as saying that דניאל avoided any anointing at all, and this includes bathing. The גמרא does not spell out exactly how bathing is included. Now both סיכה and רחיצה come from one source.

keyTerms.meaning: And I did not anoint myself at all

steps.whatToRemember: In the end, holding back from both anointing and bathing is called עינוי, based on דניאל: 'וסוך לא סכתי' (which includes bathing), together with the angel's word 'ולהתענות'.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Ashi said:
Bathing he learns from the verse itself,
as it is written: 'And I did not anoint myself at all.'
phrases.notes: The Hebrew repeats the word for anointing, and that extra wording is read to include bathing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רב זוטרא's answer after the challenge from the משנה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Bathing is included in 'וסוך לא סכתי'.

steps.title: What does 'I have come because of your words' mean?
steps.stepSummary: Taking off from the פסוקים in דניאל, the גמרא asks what the angel meant by 'I have come because of your words.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the meaning of 'and I have come because of your words'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a side topic. It asks why the angel said he came because of דניאל's words, as if he could only come because of דניאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase hints that the angel had been held back somehow and was able to return only through דניאל's prayer. The גמרא will explain this with a story.

keyTerms.meaning: I came because of your words

phrases.english: What is meant by: 'And I have come because of your words'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to a phrase from the פסוק quoted in step 20 and opens an אגדה section.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the angel's coming depended on דניאל's words.

steps.title: Starting the answer: יחזקאל's vision of the elders
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins its answer by quoting יחזקאל's vision of seventy elders offering incense and of יחזקאל being carried to ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what is written: 'And seventy men of the elders of the house of ישראל, with יאזניהו son of שפן standing among them, were standing before them, each man with his incense pan in his hand, and a thick cloud of incense was rising.' 'And He put out the form of a hand and took me by a lock of my head, and a spirit lifted me between the earth and the heavens and brought me to ירושלים in visions of God, to the entrance of the inner gate facing north, where...'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a longer answer by quoting פסוקים from יחזקאל about the elders' sinful worship in ירושלים. The quote breaks off in the middle, and the story continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These פסוקים set the scene of the sins before the חורבן, which leads into the story behind the angel's words to דניאל. The full connection to 'I have come because of your words' only becomes clear later.

keyTerms.meaning: The elders of the house of ישראל

steps.confusionAlert: This answer is not finished. The point is not yet clear here; it continues on the next part of the daf.

phrases.english: This is what is written:
'And seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel,'
'and Jaazaniah son of Shaphan standing among them,'
'were standing before them,'
'each man with his incense pan in his hand,'
'and a thick cloud of incense was rising.'
'And He put out the form of a hand,'
'and took me by a lock of my head,'
'and a spirit lifted me'
'between the earth and the heavens,'
'and brought me to Jerusalem in visions of God,'
'to the entrance of the inner gate'
'that faces north, where...'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The answer begins with יחזקאל's vision of the elders' sin in ירושלים; it is completed on the next amud.
